title: The Assumption of Mary into Heaven
summary: The Immaculate Virgin Mary, Mother of God, was assumed body and soul into heavenly glory at the end of her earthly life, a dogma infallibly defined by Pope Pius XII in Munificentissimus Deus (1950), signifying the resurrection of the body and Mary's unique participation in her Son's victory over death.

blocks.text: Introduction: The Dogma Defined

The Assumption is the dogma that the Blessed Virgin Mary, at the end of her earthly pilgrimage, was taken up body and soul into the glory of heaven. This privilege was granted to her in view of her divine motherhood and her unique cooperation in the work of redemption. Mary thus shares fully in her Son's victory over sin and death. [CCC 966]

This doctrine was solemnly defined as a dogma of faith by Pope Pius XII on November 1, 1950, in the apostolic constitution Munificentissimus Deus. The Pope declared that the Immaculate Mother of God, the ever-Virgin Mary, having completed the course of her earthly life, was assumed body and soul into heavenly glory. This definition was made ex cathedra, invoking papal infallibility. [Munificentissimus Deus]
When the perishable puts on the imperishable, and the mortal puts on immortality, then shall come to pass the saying that is written: Death is swallowed up in victory.

blocks.title: Munificentissimus Deus (1950): Dogmatic Definition
blocks.text: Pius XII infallibly defined that Mary, having completed her earthly life, was assumed body and soul into heavenly glory, invoking papal infallibility ex cathedra.
I. Biblical Foundations and Typology

While Scripture does not explicitly narrate Mary's Assumption, the doctrine is rooted in biblical typology and the logic of salvation. Mary is the New Eve, associated perfectly with the New Adam in the work of redemption. As Christ conquered death by his Resurrection, so Mary, his Mother, shares in this victory. [CCC 966]

The Ark of the Covenant, which contained the word of God and was brought by David into Jerusalem with rejoicing, is a type of Mary, who bore the Word made flesh. Psalm 132:8 speaks of the Ark being brought to God's resting place, prefiguring Mary's assumption into heaven. [Revelation 11:19, 12:1]
And a great portent appeared in heaven, a woman clothed with the sun, with the moon under her feet, and on her head a crown of twelve stars.

blocks.title: CCC 966: New Eve and Ark
blocks.text: Mary is the New Eve associated with Christ's victory over death; she is also the Ark of the New Covenant, prefigured in Scripture as brought into God's heavenly glory.
II. Theological Foundations: Divine Motherhood

The Assumption flows from Mary's divine motherhood. Because she bore God in her womb, it was fitting that her body, the temple of the Holy Spirit, should not suffer corruption. The same dignity that preserved her from original sin (Immaculate Conception) also preserved her body from the corruption of the grave. [Munificentissimus Deus 2]

Mary's perpetual virginity also points to the Assumption. Her body, which remained inviolate in giving birth to Christ, was not subject to the ordinary consequences of sin. Her Assumption is the culmination of her unique holiness and consecration to God. [CCC 966]
And the Holy Spirit will come upon you, and the power of the Most High will overshadow you; therefore the child to be born will be called holy, the Son of God.

blocks.title: Munificentissimus Deus 2: Fittingness
blocks.text: The Assumption flows from Mary's divine motherhood; it was fitting that her body, the temple of the Holy Spirit, should not suffer corruption but share in Christ's glory.
III. Mary's Cooperation in Redemption

Mary's unique cooperation in the work of redemption merited for her the privilege of the Assumption. She participated in Christ's victory over sin and death through her fiat at the Annunciation, her sufferings at the foot of the Cross, and her entire life of perfect obedience. [CCC 966]

As Mary shared intimately in Christ's redemptive work, it was fitting that she share fully in the fruits of redemption, including the resurrection of the body. The Assumption is the crown of her cooperation, the final reward for her perfect discipleship. [Lumen Gentium 59]
And a sword will pierce through your own soul also, that thoughts out of many hearts may be revealed.

blocks.title: CCC 966: Cooperation in Redemption
blocks.text: Mary's cooperation in redemption through her fiat and sufferings merited the Assumption; she shares fully in the fruits of Christ's victory, including bodily resurrection.
IV. The Question of Mary's Death

The dogmatic definition does not settle whether Mary died before being assumed. Pope Pius XII used the phrase having completed the course of her earthly life, leaving open the question of whether this included death. The majority theological opinion holds that Mary did die, in union with her Son, and was then assumed. [Munificentissimus Deus]

Those who hold that Mary died argue that it was fitting she conform to her Son in death as in life. Her death would not have been the wages of sin (since she was immaculate) but a voluntary offering in union with Christ. Others hold she was assumed without dying, by a unique privilege. Both opinions are permissible. [CCC 966]
We know that Christ being raised from the dead will never die again; death no longer has dominion over him.

blocks.title: Munificentissimus Deus: Earthly Life Completed
blocks.text: The definition leaves open whether Mary died; the majority opinion holds she died in union with Christ and was then assumed, but both opinions are theologically permissible.
V. Ancient Liturgical Tradition

The belief in Mary's Assumption is ancient, celebrated in the liturgy from the 6th century in both East and West. The Eastern Church called the feast the Dormition (Falling Asleep) of the Theotokos, emphasizing her death and assumption. The Western Church adopted the term Assumption, emphasizing her bodily glorification. [Munificentissimus Deus]

The universal celebration of this feast for over 1,500 years demonstrates the sensus fidelium, the sense of the faithful, regarding this truth. The Church's constant belief, expressed in liturgy, art, and devotion, prepared for the dogmatic definition. [CCC 966]
For behold, henceforth all generations will call me blessed.

blocks.title: CCC 966: Ancient Liturgical Feast
blocks.text: The Assumption has been celebrated in the liturgy from the 6th century in both East (Dormition) and West (Assumption), demonstrating the Church's constant belief and sensus fidelium.
VI. Papal Definition: Munificentissimus Deus (1950)

Pope Pius XII, after consulting the bishops of the world and discerning the mind of the Church, solemnly defined the dogma in Munificentissimus Deus. He declared: The Immaculate Mother of God, the ever-Virgin Mary, having completed the course of her earthly life, was assumed body and soul into heavenly glory. [Munificentissimus Deus]

The Pope invoked his apostolic authority and defined this doctrine as divinely revealed and therefore to be believed firmly and constantly by all the faithful. This was the second and most recent ex cathedra definition of papal infallibility, after the Immaculate Conception in 1854. [Vatican I, Pastor Aeternus]
And when I go and prepare a place for you, I will come again and will take you to myself, that where I am you may be also.

blocks.title: Pius XII: Ex Cathedra Definition
blocks.text: Pius XII infallibly defined the Assumption ex cathedra in 1950, the second such definition after the Immaculate Conception, declaring it divinely revealed and to be believed by all.
VII. Vatican II Reaffirmation

Vatican Council II (1962-1965) reaffirmed the dogma of the Assumption in Lumen Gentium. The Council taught that the Immaculate Virgin, preserved free from all guilt of original sin, on the completion of her earthly sojourn, was taken up body and soul into heavenly glory, and exalted by the Lord as Queen of the universe. [Lumen Gentium 59]

The Council placed the Assumption within the broader context of Mary's role in the mystery of Christ and the Church. Her Assumption is a sign of hope for the Church and a promise that all the faithful will share in the resurrection of the body. [Lumen Gentium 68-69]
Then we who are alive, who are left, shall be caught up together with them in the clouds to meet the Lord in the air; and so we shall always be with the Lord.

blocks.title: Vatican II: Queen of the Universe
blocks.text: Vatican II reaffirmed that Mary was assumed body and soul into heavenly glory and exalted as Queen of the universe, a sign of hope and promise of resurrection for all the faithful.
VIII. The Assumption and the Resurrection of the Body

The Assumption anticipates the resurrection of the body that all the faithful will experience at the end of time. Mary is the first to share fully in the fruits of Christ's Resurrection, body and soul. Her Assumption is a sign and pledge of our own future glorification. [CCC 966]

The Creed professes belief in the resurrection of the body and life everlasting. Mary's Assumption makes this truth concrete and visible, showing what God intends for all who are united to Christ. She is the eschatological icon of the Church, already glorified in body and soul. [CCC 966, 972]

But our commonwealth is in heaven, and from it we await a Savior, the Lord Jesus Christ, who will change our lowly body to be like his glorious body, by the power which enables him even to subject all things to himself.

blocks.title: CCC 966: Anticipation of Resurrection
blocks.text: Mary's Assumption anticipates the resurrection of the body; she is the first to share fully in Christ's Resurrection, a sign and pledge of our own future glorification in body and soul.
IX. Mary as Eschatological Icon of the Church

Vatican II teaches that Mary is the eschatological icon of the Church. In her Assumption, the Church contemplates what she herself is called to become: fully glorified in body and soul, united perfectly with Christ. Mary shows the destiny of all the redeemed. [Lumen Gentium 68]

The Assumption reveals the Church's ultimate hope: not merely the immortality of the soul, but the resurrection of the body and the transformation of all creation. Mary is the model and mother of the Church, leading all the faithful to her Son. [Lumen Gentium 68-69]
And I saw the holy city, new Jerusalem, coming down out of heaven from God, prepared as a bride adorned for her husband.

blocks.title: Lumen Gentium 68: Eschatological Icon
blocks.text: Mary is the eschatological icon of the Church, showing what the Church is called to become: fully glorified in body and soul, united perfectly with Christ in heavenly glory.
X. The Queenship of Mary

The Assumption is intimately connected to Mary's Queenship. Having been assumed into heaven, Mary was crowned by her Son as Queen of Heaven and Earth. Her queenship is a participation in Christ's kingship, and she reigns with him in glory, interceding for all the faithful. [Lumen Gentium 59]

Pope Pius XII established the feast of the Queenship of Mary in 1954, celebrated on August 22nd, the octave of the Assumption. Mary's queenship is not one of domination but of maternal intercession and service, conforming to her Son who came to serve, not to be served. [Ad Caeli Reginam]
On his robe and on his thigh he has a name inscribed, King of kings and Lord of lords.

blocks.title: Lumen Gentium 59: Queen of Heaven
blocks.text: Mary was crowned Queen of Heaven and Earth after her Assumption, participating in Christ's kingship and interceding maternally for all the faithful as model of service.
XI. The Feast of the Assumption

The Church celebrates the Solemnity of the Assumption on August 15th. This is a holy day of obligation in many countries, including the United States. The feast has been celebrated on this date since the 6th century, making it one of the oldest Marian feasts in the liturgical calendar. [CCC 966]

The Assumption is a day of joy and hope, celebrating Mary's victory over death and her glorification. Many Catholic cultures have special traditions, processions, and blessings on this day, expressing their devotion to the Mother of God. [CCC 971]
And Mary said, My soul magnifies the Lord, and my spirit rejoices in God my Savior.

blocks.title: CCC 966: August 15th Solemnity
blocks.text: The Solemnity of the Assumption is celebrated on August 15th, a holy day of obligation and one of the oldest Marian feasts, celebrated with joy and special devotions.
XII. Living the Faith in the Assumption

To believe in the Assumption is to affirm the dignity of the human body and the reality of the resurrection. In an age that often despises the body or denies the resurrection, Mary's Assumption proclaims that God saves us as embodied persons, not as disembodied souls. [CCC 966, 988]

The Assumption gives us hope in our own resurrection and encourages us to live with eternity in view. We are called to honor Mary by imitating her faith, obedience, and love, trusting that through her intercession we too will share in her Son's victory over death. [CCC 972, 2676]

But in fact Christ has been raised from the dead, the first fruits of those who have fallen asleep. For as by a man came death, by a man has come also the resurrection of the dead. For as in Adam all die, so also in Christ shall all be made alive.

blocks.title: CCC 988: Dignity of the Body
blocks.text: The Assumption affirms the dignity of the human body and the reality of resurrection; it gives us hope in our own glorification and calls us to imitate Mary's faith and obedience.

blocks.title: Closing Prayer: Hail Holy Queen
blocks.text: Hail, holy Queen, Mother of mercy, hail, our life, our sweetness, and our hope. To thee do we cry, poor banished children of Eve. To thee do we send up our sighs, mourning and weeping in this valley of tears. Turn then, most gracious Advocate, thine eyes of mercy toward us. And after this our exile, show unto us the blessed fruit of thy womb, Jesus. O clement, O loving, O sweet Virgin Mary. Amen.
